items.scene: Maya has one free evening. She wants to practice piano because auditions are soon, but she also wants to join her friends at a new cafe. No one is expecting her, and she has made no promise.
items.question: Which goal is Maya weighting more strongly if she chooses based on the audition being soon?
options: Keeping a prior promise to friends
Finding out what her friends intend
Predicting the exact next action she will take
items.why_this_case_matters: Two active desires compete, and no commitment settles the choice. The answer depends on which goal gets more weight.

items.scene: Leo wants to stay home and rest, but he already promised his sister he would drive her to the airport tonight. He also knows she has no backup ride.
items.question: Which factor should determine the priority in this scene?
options: The existing promise to his sister
The emotion Leo will feel afterward
The most visible action in the scene
items.why_this_case_matters: This looks like a goal conflict, but the prior promise makes it a commitment-priority case, not goal-conflict arbitration.

items.scene: Nina is hungry and wants lunch, but she also wants to finish reading one more page of her report. She closes the report and picks up her wallet.
items.question: What will Nina do next?
options: Rank lunch as morally better than work
Decide which goal matters more in general
items.why_this_case_matters: The question asks for the next action, so it belongs to action prediction rather than goal-weighting diagnosis.

items.scene: Omar wants to buy a concert ticket, but he also wants to save money for a replacement laptop. He says the laptop affects his schoolwork, while the concert would just be fun.
items.question: Which goal dominates under Omar's stated weighting rule?
options: Buying the concert ticket because it is more visible
items.why_this_case_matters: This is a direct goal tradeoff. It also guards against the shortcut of choosing the more vivid or visible action instead of the stated priority rule.
